comparisons.evidence: P's mechanisms target high-value economic bottlenecks, such as shifting to business-to-business models that unlock large institutional budgets ("schools, employers and parents"). In contrast, Q's primary service mechanism targets lower-leverage consumer transactions ("$25 paid 'reading diagnostic' session").

P establishes robust causal links, illustrating how physical stores possess a localized reverse-logistics advantage over online retail for asset grading and recirculation. Q relies on larger causal leaps, such as "Slow Ship Arbitrage," which assumes a mid-size chain can successfully undercut Amazon's massive supply chain scale through a simple lifestyle positioning.

Both outputs are highly realistic about real-world friction. P explicitly designs low-tech validation gates to bypass tech bottlenecks ("Manual pricing, condition grading, spreadsheets"), while Q systematically filters out its own high-friction concepts during its knockout round ("legal/structural friction too high for a 3-year execution window").

P provides superior precision regarding what to measure during prototyping ("returned units resell quickly enough to beat the original new-book gross profit") and maps out a highly concrete "Three-year sequence." Q outlines tests, but they lack specific success thresholds.

Both documents excel at lateral thinking by borrowing structural rules from unrelated domains. P successfully maps bookstore survival to the mechanics of "Financial exchanges" and "Clinical care," while Q establishes compelling frameworks derived from "Farmers markets" and "Gyms/fitness studios."

P covers a wide array of distinct causal pathways, including inventory risk transfer upstream, attention escrow, and IP creation. Q displays equivalent breadth, spanning shared revenue structures ("Author Equity Stakes"), data brokerages, and real-estate optimization.

P's ideation pool remains tightly focused on the actual mechanics of the book asset and the act of reading. Q dilutes its focus by including weak or generic retail tropes like converting square footage into arbitrary coworking spaces ("real product is the room") or relying on simple marketing gimmicks.
